interactions.label: Why must pralidoxime (PAM) be administered within 24–48 hours of organophosphate

params.question: Why must pralidoxime (PAM) be administered within 24–48 hours of organophosphate exposure, whereas atropine can be given at any time?

answers.text: PAM is rapidly metabolised and excreted by the kidneys after 48 hours, leaving no active drug in the body

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. PAM's time limit is not about its own metabolism. The issue is a chemical change at the enzyme — the OP–AChE bond undergoes ageing and becomes permanent, so PAM can no longer break it.

answers.text: After 24–48 hours, the OP–AChE bond undergoes ageing and becomes irreversible, so PAM can no longer reactivate the enzyme

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ageing is a chemical change that makes the OP–AChE bond permanent. Once this occurs, PAM cannot reactivate acetylcholinesterase. Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors directly and is unaffected by enzyme ageing.

answers.text: Atropine directly reactivates acetylcholinesterase, so enzyme ageing does not affect its efficacy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Atropine does NOT reactivate acetylcholinesterase — it competitively blocks muscarinic receptors to counteract excess acetylcholine. That is why it has no time limit: it works regardless of what happens to the enzyme.

answers.text: PAM is effective only against nicotinic effects, which resolve spontaneously within 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. PAM works by reactivating acetylcholinesterase, which reverses both muscarinic and nicotinic effects. Its time limit is due to enzyme ageing, not spontaneous symptom resolution.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical concept is 'ageing.' After 24–48 hours, the organophosphate–acetylcholinesterase bond undergoes a chemical change and becomes permanent. PAM can only reactivate the enzyme before this occurs. Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors directly, so enzyme ageing does not limit it.

Exactly right. Ageing is the key concept — the OP–AChE bond changes from reversible to irreversible within 24–48 hours. PAM must be given before ageing occurs; atropine works at the receptor level and has no such constraint.

interactions.label: A single intravenous dose of naloxone is sufficient to permanently reverse an op

params.question: A single intravenous dose of naloxone is sufficient to permanently reverse an opioid overdose, because naloxone binds opioid receptors more strongly than morphine or heroin.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Naloxone's duration of action is only 30–90 minutes, much shorter than most opioids. As naloxone wears off, the opioid re-occupies mu-receptors, causing re-narcotisation — making continuous monitoring and repeated dosing essential.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well spotted. Although naloxone does displace opioids at mu-receptors, its duration of action is only 30–90 minutes — far shorter than most opioids. When naloxone wears off, the opioid reclaims the receptors, causing re-narcotisation. Repeated doses and close monitoring are essential.

interactions.label: Strong acids cause coagulation necrosis, yet the tissue damage is often self-lim

params.question: Strong acids cause coagulation necrosis, yet the tissue damage is often self-limiting in depth. What explains this characteristic pattern?

answers.text: Acids are rapidly neutralised by the plasma bicarbonate buffer before reaching deeper tissues

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While the bicarbonate system buffers systemic pH, it does not neutralise a concentrated acid at the contact site. The self-limiting pattern is due to the physical protein eschar, not chemical buffering.

answers.text: The denatured protein forms a firm eschar that acts as a physical barrier, preventing the acid from penetrating deeper layers

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Coagulation necrosis produces a leathery eschar of denatured protein that physically blocks further acid penetration. This barrier effect is why acid burns, though severe on the surface, tend to be more self-limiting in depth than alkali burns.

answers.text: Acids only damage tissues with a pH below 2.0, and deeper tissues maintain a higher pH through active cellular buffering

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. There is no sharp pH threshold for acid tissue damage. The self-limiting pattern results from the physical barrier formed by coagulated surface protein, not a pH gradient in deeper tissues.

answers.text: The inflammatory response quickly dilutes the acid by increasing tissue oedema and local blood flow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The inflammatory response is secondary to the initial injury and does not prevent acid penetration. The firm, denatured protein eschar at the surface is the primary factor limiting depth of injury.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a strong acid contacts tissue, it denatures surface proteins into a firm, leathery eschar. This eschar acts as a physical barrier, limiting further penetration — the hallmark of coagulation necrosis. Different acids leave characteristic colours: black (sulphuric), yellow (nitric), white (hydrochloric).

Exactly. The eschar — a coagulated layer of denatured protein — is the hallmark of acid-induced coagulation necrosis. Remember the colour clues at the bedside: black charring (sulphuric acid), yellow xanthoproteic staining (nitric acid), and white eschar (hydrochloric acid).

interactions.label: In Amanita phalloides (death cap) poisoning, patients often appear to recover be

params.question: In Amanita phalloides (death cap) poisoning, patients often appear to recover between 24 and 48 hours after ingestion. Why is this 'false recovery' period clinically dangerous?

answers.text: The patient develops temporary immunity to amatoxin, which wears off after 48 hours, causing relapse

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. There is no immune-mediated neutralisation of amatoxin. The toxin continues to block RNA polymerase II in hepatocytes during this period, silently destroying liver cells even as gastrointestinal symptoms temporarily improve.

answers.text: Gastrointestinal symptoms resolve as initial irritation fades, but amatoxin has already blocked RNA polymerase II in hepatocytes — fulminant liver failure follows days later

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Amatoxin halts transcription by blocking RNA polymerase II, progressively destroying hepatocytes. The initial GI symptoms fade, creating a deceptive window of apparent recovery, while irreversible hepatic damage continues silently.

answers.text: The toxin undergoes enterohepatic recirculation and re-enters the gut after 48 hours, triggering a second, more severe episode

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Although some enterohepatic recirculation may occur, the false recovery is not caused by toxin leaving and returning. It reflects a gap between resolving GI irritation and the delayed onset of hepatic failure from ongoing hepatocyte destruction.

answers.text: A second, more lethal toxin in the mushroom is absorbed more slowly and reaches peak concentration only at 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Amanita phalloides exerts its lethal effect through amatoxin alone. The false recovery reflects a temporal gap between early GI symptoms and delayed hepatotoxicity from the same toxin, not a second poison.

overallFeedback.feedback: Amatoxin blocks RNA polymerase II in hepatocytes, halting protein synthesis. GI symptoms improve between 24–48 hours, creating a dangerous illusion of recovery. Meanwhile, liver destruction is progressing silently — fulminant hepatic failure follows. Never discharge these patients during the false recovery window.

Correct. Amatoxin blocks RNA polymerase II, halting protein synthesis in hepatocytes. The key clinical rule: symptom onset after 6 hours suggests amatoxin. The 24–48 hour false recovery is a classic trap — never discharge a suspected amatoxin patient during this window.

interactions.label: A 28-year-old farmer ingests paraquat and arrives at the emergency department wi

params.question: A 28-year-old farmer ingests paraquat and arrives at the emergency department within one hour, appearing deceptively well. The junior resident asks which specific antidote to start. What is the correct response?

answers.text: Start pralidoxime and atropine — paraquat is a pesticide, so the standard organophosphate protocol applies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Paraquat is a herbicide, not an organophosphate. It does not inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so atropine and pralidoxime have no role. Misclassifying paraquat as an organophosphate is a dangerous error.

answers.text: Administer N-acetylcysteine to protect against the oxidative lung damage caused by paraquat

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Although N-acetylcysteine is an antioxidant used in paracetamol poisoning, it has no established role in paraquat management. There is no specific antidote for paraquat — management is strictly supportive.

answers.text: There is no specific antidote for paraquat — management is supportive care only, and supplemental oxygen must be withheld

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Paraquat causes fatal pulmonary fibrosis through superoxide radical generation via redox cycling. No antidote exists. Critically, supplemental oxygen accelerates the lung injury and must be avoided.

answers.text: Give hydroxocobalamin to neutralise the free radicals generated by paraquat's redox cycling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Hydroxocobalamin is the antidote for cyanide poisoning — it binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin. It has no role in paraquat management. No agent effectively neutralises paraquat's redox cycling.

overallFeedback.feedback: Paraquat has no specific antidote. It causes lethal pulmonary fibrosis through superoxide radical generation (redox cycling). Management is supportive care only. Remember: supplemental oxygen must be avoided — it accelerates the very lung injury that kills the patient.

Exactly right. Paraquat is the one poison in this lecture with no specific antidote. Management is entirely supportive — and the critical additional point is that supplemental oxygen must be withheld, as it worsens pulmonary fibrosis through enhanced redox cycling.
